newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong official defends "unfair" election laws.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong official defends "unfair" election laws.

text.p: A senior Hong Kong official denied on Saturday that a new election law would curtail democracy in the territory despite the move depriving two million people of the right to vote.

Speaking on a radio talk show, Constitutional Affairs Secretary Michael Suen said Hong Kong would see more democracy in a decade according to the Basic Law, the territory's post-colonial constitution.
He said the Basic Law stipulated that a review would be carried out on whether all 60 Legislative Council seats should be directly elected.

At present, only a third of the 60 seats are returned by geographical constituencies. Under the new rules, the remaining 40 seats will be filled next May by representatives from business and professional bodies in so-called functional constituencies, and by an election committee made up of pro-China politicians, businessmen and professionals.
"After 2007, Hong Kong people can decide whether all 60 seats will be directly elected," Suen said.
But listeners who phoned in to the show gave Suen an ear full, calling the election law unfair and undemocratic.

"Businessmen, industrialists and professionals will have three votes. They have a vote in the geographic constituencies, a vote in the functional constituencies and a vote in the election committee," a listener said.
"But people from the grassroots can only have one ballot, which does not even allow them a say on who they can elect as the voting system will be proportional representation," the listener said.

Under Friday's published election law, more than two million people who were eligible to vote in the 1995's functional constituencies would be disenfranchised. They would be replaced by corporate votes adding up to no more than 200,000 ballots.

For geographical constituencies, Hong Kong will be divided into five areas each with four seats. This contrasts with arrangements in the 1995 election where the territory was divided into 20 smaller districts, each with one seat.
The popular Democratic Party has criticised the change as favouring less popular pro-Beijing parties.
Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule on July 1, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
